parole.significato: Forming adjectives from nouns, indicating that something belongs to, resembles, is characterized by, is suited for, or…
parole.testo: Inherited from Proto-Germanic *-īnaz (“belonging to, characterized by, made of”), an adjective-forming suffix. Compare Norwegian Nynorsk -en, Danish -en, Swedish -en, German -en and English -en (“adjective-forming suffix”).
From glinse. Cognate with Norwegian Bokmål glans, through Proto-Germanic *glend-.

parole.significato: a blackfly (any member of the Simuliidae)
parole.testo: Cognate with Swedish knott, English gnat and maybe Russian гнус (gnus). Inherited from Proto-Germanic *gnattaz
From Proto-Germanic *luppǭ (“flea, sandflea”, originally “jumper”), from Proto-Germanic *luppijaną (“to jump, dart”).

From Proto-Germanic *lungô (“the light organ”), from Proto-Indo-European *lengʷʰ- (“light, agile, nimble”). Compare Dutch long, English lung, Danish lunge, German Lunge, Swedish lunga, Icelandic lunga.
From Proto-Germanic *nasō, from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂s-, and Old Norse nǫs.

parole.significato: rust; a reddish-brown coating of hydrated iron oxides or iron hydroxides formed on iron or steel through oxidation
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *rustaz (“rust”), from Proto-Indo-European *rudʰso- (“red”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁rewdʰ- (“red”). Related to rød (“red”). Compare Norwegian Nynorsk rust, Danish rust, Swedish rost, Dutch roest, German Rost and English rust.

parole.significato: a schilling, the old currency of Austria, divided into 100 groschen
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *skillingaz. Doublet of shilling and skilling.

parole.significato: the act or process of setting, placing, or deploying something
parole.testo: From sette (“to set, put, place”), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *satjaną (“to set, place”), from Proto-Indo-European *sodéyeti (“to cause to sit”), the causative of *sed- (“to sit”). parole.significato: to glance, especially quickly, sideways, or furtively
parole.testo: Possibly from skue (“to look, behold”), which is inherited from Old Norse skoða (“to look at, examine”), from Proto-Germanic *skuþōną (“to view”), related to *skawwōną (“to look”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *(s)kewh₁- (“to perceive”).
